The Adaptive Convexity Framework

Part 4 of 6 · ≈ 16 min read · In pictures · 4 exhibits →

Tax Architecture & ROC Strategy

The Hidden Multiplier

Wrapper engineering as a structural edge.

Part 3 chose the convexity backbone. Part 4 asks the next question: once you own convexity, how much of it do you get to keep? Sell one large, long-held winner from a taxable account and taxes can take 15 to 35 percent or more of the gain, depending on income, the net investment income tax (NIIT) and state tax; realize gains every year along the way and the bill is larger. Wrapper engineering routes each dollar to the that minimize lifetime tax friction and keep intact.

Conventional guidance takes the pre-tax deduction first, treats Roth as a side account for younger savers, and fills taxable once the limits are full, an order built to shrink this year’s tax bill. Wrapper engineering is built for the number you end with. Over decades, especially when gains are realized along the way, tax treatment can rival what asset selection adds, and sometimes exceed it. So the framework treats wrapper placement as a structural return multiplier and gives it the same rigor as asset selection and position sizing.

Jurisdiction scope. The examples use United States accounts: Roth accounts, the taxable brokerage account, and pre-tax plans such as a traditional 401(k) or IRA. The logic carries to other countries once you substitute the local tax-advantaged accounts: put the positions you expect to sell where selling costs least, and spend scarce tax-advantaged room on the holdings that gain most from it.

A mediocre asset in an optimal wrapper can produce superior terminal wealth compared with an exceptional asset in a suboptimal one.

Among the thinkers the framework draws on (Part 2), Edelman makes the long-horizon case for why tax treatment matters, and none of them formalizes wrapper routing; the framework fills that gap deliberately.

Wrapper Engineering North Star

  • Maximize Roth capacity, and spend it on convexity you may rotate. For positions you may rebalance, rotate out of a sector or exit when a thesis breaks, tax-free compounding over thirty to sixty years can outweigh most other decisions you make about them.
  • Convert strategically, not blindly. Building Roth balances early, and converting pre-tax money in low-income years, shrinks the pre-tax balance that required minimum distributions (RMDs) will later force out, along with the income-related Medicare surcharges those withdrawals can trigger.

The Three Containers

Three wrappers, three roles.

Each of the three kinds of account has a job, and one rule assigns them: match what a position is expected to do (the shape of its payoff and how likely you are to sell it) to the account whose tax treatment rewards that behavior.

Wrapper treatment and the payoff profile each is matched to
Wrapper Tax treatment Matched role
Roth accountsTax-free growth and qualified withdrawals that may rotate
Taxable accountsTax on realized gains and distributionsBitcoin backbone, return-of-capital , buy-and-hold positions beyond Roth capacity, harvesting satellites
Pre-tax accountsTax-deferred; taxed as income on withdrawalEmployer match; deferrals in an unusually high-income year; ordinary-income payers where pre-tax space exists

Roth suits positions that may be rotated tax-free · taxable suits never-sold holdings and return-of-capital income · pre-tax is tactical, not structural

Bitcoin, held in cold storage under a never-sell rule, belongs in taxable; the Roth section below gives the reasons, and Part 3 charts its path from accumulation to borrowing. Everything else follows a sequence for each new dollar, with no fixed split.

  1. Capture the employer match first. Contribute at least enough to earn the full employer match. Your own contribution can go into a Roth 401(k) bucket if the plan has one. The match itself is pre-tax unless the plan lets you elect Roth matching contributions, which SECURE 2.0 permits if the plan adopts it (the match must be fully vested and is taxable income in the year it is made).

  2. Maximize the Roth IRA next. For 2026, direct contributions phase out between $153,000 and $168,000 of modified adjusted gross income for single filers ($242,000 to $252,000 joint). Above that, a backdoor Roth (a non-deductible traditional IRA contribution converted to Roth) keeps the door open under current law, subject to the pro-rata rule if you hold other pre-tax IRA balances.

  3. Route remaining capital by position type. Torque that may rotate goes to Roth: past the Roth IRA, that means Roth 401(k) deferrals and, where the plan allows it, a mega backdoor. Return-of-capital Ballast, buy-and-hold positions beyond your Roth room, and harvesting satellites go to taxable. Ordinary-income payers, such as bond funds and REITs whose distributions are not return of capital, go to pre-tax where you have pre-tax space. In an unusually high-income year, your 401(k) or 403(b) deferrals go pre-tax too, for conversion to Roth later (the pre-tax section explains).

The sequence governs where each new dollar goes. Separately, the dashboard’s Framework Integrity Score (Part 6) measures the household’s dollar split against the FIS wrapper targets of 45 percent Roth, 35 percent taxable and 20 percent pre-tax, and charges a small Allocation penalty (at most about 6 of its 100 points) once the split drifts more than 10 points from them (as of September 2026; the formula is on the Math page). A book routed by this sequence can show that drift: the 45/35/20 split is a scoring parameter, not a Part 4 rule.

Tax-Free Convexity

Reserving Roth for Torque.

Roth capacity is scarce. The 2026 IRA limit is $7,500 per person ($8,600 at 50 or older), shared across traditional and Roth IRAs. It caps the Roth IRA, not Roth space as a whole: a Roth 401(k) takes up to $24,500 of your own deferrals in 2026 (more from age 50, with catch-up contributions), and where the plan allows after-tax contributions and converts them, a mega backdoor can add more, up to the $72,000 federal limit on everything added to the plan in a year (your deferrals and the employer’s contributions count toward it).

Compound interest has been called the eighth wonder of the world. Tax-free compound interest is the ninth. The framework’s cornerstone allocation principle follows: spend scarce Roth room on the highest-conviction Torque that may rotate, where tax-free compounding and tax-free trading do the most work. Consider the mathematics.

The gap between what each wrapper lets you keep is small on an ordinary gain and wide on a right-tail one, so placement matters most exactly where convexity is largest. The comparison below works the case of a gain realized once; Part 5 works the case of gains realized every year, and later Parts point back to these two.

A Roth keeps essentially all of a gain, since qualified withdrawals are not taxed. A taxable account that sells keeps roughly 75 to 85 percent of the gain after long-term capital gains tax and the NIIT, depending on income; the exhibit uses the top federal rate of 23.8 percent, the rate a large one-time sale meets. A pre-tax account keeps roughly 60 to 80 percent of the whole withdrawal, principal included, because every dollar comes out as ordinary income; the exhibit uses a blended 30 percent for withdrawals spread over retirement. On a position that grows tenfold, the Roth ends about 27 percent ahead of the taxable account that sells it, and on a single sale that lead never passes about 31 percent however large the gain. Hold the taxable position until death instead, and under current law a stepped-up basis can close the gap almost entirely. All of these figures are federal and illustrative; they depend on income, filing status, state tax and the rules in force when you sell or withdraw.

One caveat: the exhibit leaves out the deduction a pre-tax contribution earns going in. At the same tax rate going in and coming out, a Roth and a pre-tax account leave you the same after-tax money, whatever the return. Four things tip convex, right-tail positions toward Roth. Contribution limits are set in dollars, so a full Roth contribution shelters more after-tax money than a full pre-tax one. A large pre-tax balance comes out through required distributions, which can push it into higher brackets than the deduction saved. The original owner never takes required distributions from a Roth. And heirs generally inherit a Roth free of income tax under current law. The gap that grows with the size of the win in every case is Roth against a taxable account that sells.

Roth also eases three retirement risks: a withdrawal in a high-tax year, a guess about tax rates decades out, and a forced withdrawal in a downturn. Under current law, qualified withdrawals are tax-free whatever your income. Early Roth IRA withdrawals have rules of their own: contributions come out tax-free at any time, earnings are tax-free once you are 59 and a half and five tax years have passed since the year of your first Roth IRA contribution, and each conversion starts its own five-year clock for the 10 percent additional tax on converted money withdrawn before 59 and a half.

Roth Allocation Discipline

  • Bitcoin is held outside Roth by default. Three reasons. It is never sold, so tax-free trading buys it nothing, and under current law (IRC §1014) a taxable holding that passes at death generally takes a stepped-up basis, so the gain built up during life is not taxed as income. Only a taxable holding can be pledged for a loan: using an IRA as security for a loan counts as a distribution (IRC §408(e)(4)). And Roth room is scarce and better spent on Torque that may rotate. Holding, borrowing against and bequeathing an appreciated asset is the buy-borrow-die approach Part 3 teaches; a loan adds interest cost and the risk of a forced sale, which is a taxable one.
  • Conviction with restraint. Tax-free trading is why rotating positions live here. It is no reason to trade more often. When to rotate is guided by scoring, developed in Part 6.

Case Study: Roth Prioritization (Illustrative)

A 35-year-old earning $140,000 puts the full $7,500 into a Roth IRA every year, invests it in high-conviction Torque, and rotates as theses evolve. Every exit is tax-free, so every exit redeploys at full value. On a hypothetical return of about 15.5 percent a year, invested at the start of each year and used here only for illustration, the Roth reaches roughly $4.2 million after 30 years, with nothing owed on gains or withdrawals. Run the same positions on the same path in a taxable account that realizes about a twentieth of its accumulated gain each year, taxed at 15 to 20 percent, and it finishes roughly $440,000 to $580,000 behind, about 11 to 14 percent of terminal wealth lost to placement alone. That is before any tax on the gains still unrealized at the end; pay it and the gap roughly doubles. Actual returns depend on position selection and market conditions.

Why fill the Roth IRA before putting more Roth money into the workplace plan? Plan menus usually offer a short list of funds, while a Roth IRA at a brokerage can hold the individual positions and rotations the framework relies on. Position sizing, diversification and rotation mechanics are in Part 5.

Roth overlay · Doctrine · defined-risk only

Options within the Roth: purchased convexity only.

A Roth may hold long calls, long puts and defined-risk spreads, never naked options, short volatility or any other undefined-risk strategy. Purchased options are tactical overlays for a high-conviction thesis, with the loss limited to the premium paid; they are neither core holdings nor income generators. Much of the time their expected value is negative, because time decay usually costs more than the moves repay, so they earn a place only when conviction justifies a defined-risk, asymmetric bet. Two representative uses: a long-dated call on an infrastructure theme early in its adoption, or a long put as portfolio insurance during systemic stress.

Sizing And Survivability

  • Hard cap of 3 to 5 percent of Roth account value, measured as the maximum loss at entry, which is the premium paid. In a $75,000 Roth, that caps at-risk capital at $2,250 to $3,750.
  • Survivability before profitability. A purchased option can lose its full premium. Sized correctly, that loss is affordable; oversized, it does real damage.

Income, Ballast, and Harvesting

The work taxable accounts do.

Taxable accounts hold what does not need Roth’s tax-free trading. Yield never qualifies a position as Ballast; Part 5’s tests do. Among holdings that pass them, the taxable account favors those whose distributions are characterized as , ideally paid monthly or more often, because that character defers the tax and leaves more cash to deploy into Bitcoin accumulation or tactical rotation without selling anything.

The framework’s named income-Ballast instrument is STRC, Strategy Inc.’s variable-rate perpetual preferred stock. As of January 2026 it paid 11 percent a year in monthly distributions, historically characterized as return of capital; that characterization is set each tax year and verified on Form 1099-DIV. STRC qualifies as Ballast under the three-of-five rule on durable cash generation (for a preferred, its distribution record: paid in every period since issuance), low factor correlation (the monthly rate reset is designed to hold its price near its $100 stated amount) and a liquidity-resilient valuation (its $100 stated amount and rate-reset support). It carries no agency credit rating as a new instrument; the framework reads the issuer’s Bitcoin asset coverage as its measure of balance-sheet strength.

Update, September 2026. On June 26, 2026, during a Bitcoin selloff, STRC closed at $74.57 (intraday low $71.25). It was back above $84 by June 30 and closed at $99.56 on September 29, close to its 52-week high of $100.42. Distributions were paid throughout; the rate is now 12 percent a year, paid semi-monthly.

The mechanism underneath is deferral. A return-of-capital distribution is not taxed when you receive it; it lowers your cost basis (IRC §301(c)(2)). Once basis reaches zero, further return-of-capital distributions are taxed as capital gain when received (§301(c)(3)). The deferred gain is taxed when you sell, unless a step-up at death resets the basis first. Your broker reports these distributions on Form 1099-DIV, Box 3 (nondividend distributions), and the issuer files Form 8937 describing the basis effect.

The deferral is only as good as the instrument paying it.

Credit and issuer concentration

The distribution depends entirely on the issuer’s financial health and capital management.

Interest-rate sensitivity

Rising rates or widening credit spreads can pressure preferred valuations.

Classification risk

Return-of-capital treatment is set each tax year and can change with the issuer’s results, turning tax-deferred distributions into taxable dividends.

Correlation under stress

Bitcoin drawdowns can compress the issuer’s distributable income and STRC’s market price.

No maturity

The perpetual structure offers no guaranteed return of principal.

Taxable mechanics · Losses become durable tax assets

Tax-loss harvesting.

A realized loss offsets capital gains and up to $3,000 of ordinary income a year ($1,500 if married filing separately), and net losses beyond that carry forward. Return-of-capital distributions steadily lower basis, which makes harvestable losses less likely, not impossible; such a position is held for basis step-up rather than harvesting. The framework’s harvesting candidates are tactical satellites, kept at satellite size. Bitcoin is left off the list: a harvest is a sale, and the accumulate-only rule in Part 3 makes no exception for one. Directly held Bitcoin is not covered by the wash-sale rule under current law. On September 16, 2026 the House Ways and Means Committee advanced H.R. 10357, the Digital Asset Tax Certainty Act, 38 to 5. As approved, it would extend the rule to digital assets sold after September 14, 2026, the day it was introduced, so a loss taken now could still be caught if it is enacted. It is not law.

  1. Review quarterly for material losses. List taxable positions down more than 20 percent from cost basis.

  2. Harvest where the thesis holds. If the thesis is intact, realize the loss and redeploy at once into a similar position that is not substantially identical. The wash-sale rule disallows the loss if you buy substantially identical stock or securities within 30 days before or after the sale (IRC §1091). The disallowed loss is normally added to the replacement’s basis, so it is deferred; if the repurchase happens in your IRA or Roth IRA, the loss is lost for good (Rev. Rul. 2008-5). Check every account before you harvest. If the thesis is breaking, harvest and redeploy to a higher-conviction opportunity.

  3. Track carryforwards as durable assets. Harvested losses shelter future gains for years; keep a record so none is lost.

Margin: An Optional Overlay

  • Conditional, not structural. When income-producing positions yield more than the margin rate, the spread is positive carry, and it lasts only while that holds; a change in the rate regime can reverse it. Compare the two after tax: margin interest is deductible only as investment interest, up to your net investment income and only if you itemize (IRC §163(d)), and return-of-capital distributions are not investment income.
  • Revocable by design. Margin is a broker privilege that can be repriced or withdrawn during stress. Borrowing rates float and can spike, and a fall in collateral can force a sale at the worst moment; a forced sale is also a taxable one. Nothing in the framework depends on margin. The framework publishes no margin sizing rules of its own. The loan-to-value arithmetic and the deleveraging rules for borrowing against Bitcoin are in Part 3, and the arithmetic applies to margin too.

Tactical, Not Structural

Pre-tax accounts: inferior, occasionally useful.

For long-duration convex positions, pre-tax accounts have four drawbacks. Every dollar that comes out, gains included, is taxed as ordinary income, so a right-tail win never gets the long-term capital gains rate it would have had in taxable; the deduction going in is the other side of that trade (see the caveat under the Tax Wedge). RMDs start at age 73, or at 75 for anyone born in 1960 or later, under current law, and they force taxable withdrawals whether you need the money or not. Heirs generally owe income tax on what they withdraw, with no step-up in basis. And withdrawals before age 59 and a half generally incur a 10 percent additional tax on top of income tax.

Gross Is Not Net

A pre-tax balance is a joint claim between you and the government. The tax is deferred, not forgiven, and the dollars you owe rise with every dollar of gain. At a constant rate the split holds; the owed share grows only if a larger balance is withdrawn at higher brackets or forced out by required distributions. A Roth settles the government’s claim up front, so under current law every later dollar of growth is yours.

The exhibit below splits one balance into both claims; read the deferred tax as a second position riding inside your balance.

Pre-tax accounts still earn their place in three cases.

  1. Capture the employer match, always

    A dollar-for-dollar match, once it vests, is an immediate 100 percent return on the money you put in (a 50-cent match is 50 percent), and no wrapper preference outweighs that, which is why it is step 1 of the routing sequence.

  2. Arbitrage an unusually high-income year

    When a one-time income spike lifts your marginal rate well above normal, pre-tax 401(k) or 403(b) deferrals take the tax break at the higher rate, to be converted to Roth in a later, lower-bracket year (through an in-plan Roth conversion if the plan offers one, or after the money is rolled over to an IRA). The captured value is roughly the rate spread applied to the amount converted. A traditional IRA is the wrong tool for this: in such a year its contribution is usually not deductible for anyone covered by a workplace plan (2026 phase-outs: $81,000–$91,000 single; $129,000–$149,000 joint when the contributor is covered), it shares the $7,500 IRA limit step 2 already used, and a year-end traditional IRA balance brings the pro-rata rule into a backdoor Roth.

  3. Hold ordinary-income payers where pre-tax space exists

    Bond funds and REITs whose distributions are not return of capital would pay ordinary-rate tax every year in a taxable account. If you already have pre-tax space, such as a workplace plan or a rollover IRA, they belong there, leaving Roth room for Torque.

Under Uncertain Rules

Built for changing tax law.

Everything above rests on rules Congress can rewrite: contribution limits, income thresholds, distribution ages, deduction rules, step-up at death, the wash-sale rule, tax rates, and the tax-free status of Roth withdrawals itself. The framework assumes none is permanent. Its routing usually leaves money in more than one kind of account (the employer match and ordinary-income payers often land in pre-tax), and that spread limits how much damage any single change can do.

The two tax-advantaged accounts are exposed differently. Roth money has already paid tax at a known rate, so an adverse change would be new tax on capital that was taxed once already. Pre-tax money has paid nothing yet, so an adverse change raises or accelerates a bill that was always coming. Roth rules carry no guarantee; the framework favors Roth because, under legislative uncertainty, it has the better risk asymmetry of the two.

This part decides where each kind of holding lives; what to hold, how large, and when to rotate belong to Part 5 and Part 6.

Scope

Tax and leverage treatments described here reflect current United States law as of September 2026 and are subject to legislative change; step-up in basis, borrow-against strategies, and wash-sale treatment in particular are policy-dependent and not guaranteed. Where this part names a security, such as STRC, it illustrates how the framework applies its own criteria; it is not a recommendation for your situation. This framework does not constitute tax, legal, or financial advice. Consult qualified professionals for your specific situation.

End of Part 4

Part 4 matched each holding to the account whose tax treatment rewards what it is expected to do, and judged each placement by what you keep after tax over decades.
